A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 16 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2, including figures, tables, equations and appendices, support comparison. The added table inconsistencies are document-level reporting problems, not missing evidence.

before.justification: V1 reports original alignment diagnostics and experiments on slot filling, machine translation and JSON generation, with ablations and per-language appendix results.

after.justification: V2 retains these original empirical results and adds experiments on broader alignment-language coverage and simultaneous alignment at multiple layers.

M1.justification: The alternating task/contrastive training procedure, LoRA architecture and Equation 1 remain unchanged. V2 adds an experimental variant applying alignment losses at multiple layers (Section 5.2 and Appendix F), extending the single-layer variants evaluated in v1.

E1.justification: V2 expands alignment-training coverage to all 19 non-English languages in the paper's slot-filling evaluation and available pairs among all 20 languages. Section 6.1 introduces oracle scenarios where every transfer language has parallel alignment data. The downstream datasets, tasks and evaluation languages remain unchanged.

E2.justification: V2 Section 3 newly reports a qualitative comparison favoring alternating over combined-loss joint optimization, without numerical scores. Table 3 also adds SFT baseline rows to the layer-placement comparison. The main comparison methods remain unchanged; newly cited alignment methods are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: Added experiments use 38 English-linked directional pairs or 238 available multilingual pairs and test alignment losses at multiple layers. Existing splits, metrics, model sizes and stated training hyperparameters are retained. The exact multi-layer configuration is inconsistently labeled between Appendix F and Table 13.

E4.justification: New Table 4 tests whether broader alignment coverage and additional non-English connections improve transfer. Section 5.2 and Appendix F test whether aligning multiple layers improves over single-layer alignment. The resource-level, domain-generalization, merging and long-sequence analyses already present in v1 are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the correlation significance statement and dispersion across transfer languages. V2 clarifies Table 3's standard-deviation caption but adds no repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or statistical testing procedures.

E6.justification: Original Table 2 and corresponding existing results remain unchanged. New Table 4 reports transfer F1 of 63.6 under both expanded alignment settings, versus 61.7 for the retained smaller configuration. Multi-layer results and a top-layer per-language row are added, although the latter duplicates middle-layer scores in Table 11 and conflicts with Table 3.

T1.justification: Equation 1, the retrieval formulation and existing mathematical reasoning remain unchanged. The new optimization and alignment explanations are qualitative; no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or substantive derivations are introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same central claims about middle-layer alignment, improved cross-lingual transfer, generalization beyond aligned languages and merging separately trained modules. Added supporting analyses do not replace or broaden these core claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations involving reduced gradient conflicts under alternating optimization and implicit multiway alignment through English. It identifies multi-layer alignment gains as task-dependent and expands the Chinese JSON-generation failure explanation using fixed-length representations and longer token sequences. The original principal limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly identifies HoreKa as a computing resource and explicitly notes that typographical errors in the original prompts were preserved. Appendix D's hyperparameters, decoding procedure and merging weights, and the code/data access instructions, otherwise remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands research positioning. Section 7 acknowledges related middle-layer findings and adds detailed comparisons with Mao and Yu, Zhong et al., and Kargaran et al., replacing v1's brief treatment of nearby representation research. It explicitly distinguishes the decoder-only alignment contribution from established contrastive learning and adds discussion of alternative alignment mechanisms and modular cross-lingual training.

P1.justification: V2 adds method subheadings and explanations, a larger-scale alignment subsection, Appendix F and acknowledgments, and expands related-work prose. Terminology and cross-references receive limited editing. The overall narrative and section sequence remain recognizable, without extensive document-wide rewriting.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 4 and 13, expands the per-language slot-filling table, adds SFT rows to Table 3 and elaborates several captions. Existing figures receive small label or caption edits, and tables reflow between pages. New Table 13 contains a malformed, unlabeled slot-filling row and inconsistent layer labeling.

improvement.justification: The expanded research positioning and larger-scale alignment comparison provide a modest gain in context and practical evidence while preserving the original main results. This benefit is partly offset by new appendix errors: Table 11 duplicates middle- and top-layer scores despite different Table 3 aggregates, and Table 13 has a malformed row and conflicts with Appendix F's layer description. These problems weaken the added layer analysis, limiting the overall improvement.
